source: RL Circuits
The current rises as I = (ε/R)(1 − e^(−Rt/L)), with time constant L/R.
Students think the current jumps to ε/R the instant the switch closes.

Put an inductor in series with a resistor and a battery. Because the inductor fights every change in current, the current cannot jump when the switch closes; it grows smoothly, in a curve you have seen before in charging a capacitor.

Loop rule, with the inductor's back emf: $\varepsilon - IR - L\dfrac{dI}{dt} = 0$, so
        $$\frac{dI}{dt} = \frac{\varepsilon - IR}{L} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dI}{\varepsilon/R - I} = \frac{R}{L}\,dt.$$
        Integrating from $I = 0$ at $t = 0$ gives $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right)$. At first $I = 0$, so the whole battery voltage sits across the inductor: the current starts rising at the rate $\varepsilon/L$. As $I$ grows, more voltage goes to the resistor and the rise slows.

$$I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right), \qquad V_L = \varepsilon e^{-t/\tau}, \qquad \tau = \frac{L}{R}.$$
        If the battery is removed and the loop stays closed through a resistance $R$, the current dies away as $I = I_0e^{-t/\tau}$.
An RL circuit after the switch closes: the current starts at zero and rises toward $\varepsilon/R$, while the inductor's voltage starts at $\varepsilon$ and fades.
The same circuit drawn with its parts, the current shown as moving dots.
Worked examples
A $0.50\ \text{H}$ inductor and a $10\ \Omega$ resistor are switched onto $12\ \text{V}$. Find $\tau$, the final current, the current after one time constant and the starting rate of rise.
Current after one time constant
$I(\tau) \approx 0.759\ \text{A}$
$\tau = L/R = 0.50/10 = 50.0\ \text{ms}$; final current $\varepsilon/R = 1.2\ \text{A}$.
At $t = 0$: $\dfrac{dI}{dt} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{L} = \dfrac{12}{0.50} = 24\ \text{A/s}$.
When does the current in that circuit reach 90% of its final value?
Time to 90%
$t \approx 115\ \text{ms}$
After the current has settled at $1.2\ \text{A}$, the battery is removed and the inductor and resistor are left connected. What is the current $50\ \text{ms}$ later?
Switching off gently
$I \approx 0.441\ \text{A}$
Loop rule without the battery: $L\dfrac{dI}{dt} = -IR$, so $I = I_0e^{-t/\tau}$ with the same $\tau = 50\ \text{ms}$.
$I = 1.2e^{-1} = 0.441\ \text{A}$. The inductor keeps the current flowing for a while after the battery is gone.

"The current jumps to $\varepsilon/R$ the instant the switch closes." A sudden jump would need an infinite $dI/dt$, and so an infinite back emf. Instead the inductor takes the whole battery voltage at the start and the current begins at zero. Check with the loop rule at $t = 0$: $I = 0$, so $L\,dI/dt = \varepsilon$. (A capacitor is the opposite: its current jumps at once and its voltage builds slowly.)
